20 End-of-Chapter MCQs Key Points

1. Introduction

Tintinalli Ch.194 p.1270
  • β-blockers are widely prescribed for cardiovascular disease (HTN, AF, post-MI), HF, migraine prophylaxis, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, anxiety, and esophageal varices.
  • Among the leading drug classes for ED toxicology — combined with CCBs, account for >65% of cardiovascular medication overdose deaths.
  • Toxicity may occur from intentional overdose, accidental pediatric ingestion, or therapeutic misadventures (drug interactions, renal/hepatic impairment).
  • "One pill can kill" in toddlers — particularly with potent agents (propranolol, sotalol).

2. Pharmacology & Receptor Effects

Tintinalli Table 194-1, Fig 194-1 p.1270–1271

β-Adrenergic receptors

📚 Table 194-1 — Location and Activity of β-Adrenergic Receptors (β1/β2/β3) (Tintinalli p.1270)
ReceptorPrimary locationStimulation effectAntagonism (β-blocker)
β₁Heart, kidney↑ HR, ↑ contractility, renin release↓ HR, ↓ contractility, ↓ AV conduction
β₂Bronchial smooth muscle, skeletal muscle, liver, vesselsBronchodilation, glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis, vasodilationBronchospasm, hypoglycemia, vasoconstriction
β₃Adipose tissue, skeletal muscleLipolysis, thermogenesisInhibits lipolysis

Cardiac signaling

📚 Fig 194-1 — Cardiac myocyte β-receptor and calcium signaling: β-receptor → Gs → adenylate cyclase → ↑ cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates L-type Ca²⁺ channels + ryanodine receptors → ↑ contractility (Tintinalli p.1271)

How β-blockers cause toxicity

  • Loss of inotropic and chronotropic support from β₁ blockade → bradycardia + decreased cardiac output → hypotension.
  • Some β-blockers also have membrane-stabilizing (Na-channel blocking) activity — produce wide QRS like TCA: propranolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, oxprenolol.
  • Sotalol additionally has Class III antiarrhythmic activity (K-channel block) → QT prolongation + torsades.
  • Lipophilic β-blockers (especially propranolol, also metoprolol, carvedilol) → CNS penetration → seizures, coma.
  • β₂ blockade → hypoglycemia (especially in children, diabetics on insulin) + bronchospasm.
Pearl — propranolol is the worst β-blocker overdose: highly lipid-soluble (CNS effects: seizures, coma) + Na-channel-blocking (wide QRS) + non-selective (β₁+β₂). Mortality is highest with propranolol overdose.
Inline MCQ 1. Which β-blocker has the WORST overdose mortality due to combined CNS, Na-channel, and full β-blockade?
A. Atenolol
B. Metoprolol
C. Propranolol (lipid-soluble + Na-channel block + non-selective)
D. Bisoprolol
Answer: C. Propranolol — high lipophilicity (CNS toxicity: seizures, coma) + membrane stabilization (wide QRS) + non-selective. Worst overdose. Reference: Tintinalli p.1271–1272.

3. β-Blocker Pharmacologic Profiles

Tintinalli Table 194-2 p.1272
📚 Table 194-2 — β-Blocker Profiles: selectivity, lipophilicity, partial agonism (ISA), protein binding, sodium-channel blockade, half-life, max daily dose (Tintinalli p.1272)

Properties to know

  • Selectivity (β₁ vs β₂):
    • β₁-selective ("cardioselective"): atenolol, metoprolol, esmolol, betaxolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol, acebutolol — safer in asthma at therapeutic doses (selectivity lost at high overdose levels).
    • Non-selective: propranolol, nadolol, timolol, sotalol — bronchospasm risk.
    • Combined α + β: labetalol, carvedilol — cause vasodilation + bradycardia.
  • Lipophilicity: high → CNS penetration (propranolol, metoprolol, carvedilol, nebivolol) → seizures/coma.
  • Partial agonism (intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, ISA): pindolol, acebutolol, oxprenolol, penbutolol — less bradycardia/hypotension in overdose; may even cause tachycardia/HTN.
  • Membrane-stabilizing (Na-channel block): propranolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, oxprenolol → wide QRS like TCA → NaHCO₃ helpful.
  • Class III antiarrhythmic (K-channel): sotalol → QT prolongation, torsades.
  • Half-life: sotalol (12 h) and atenolol (6–9 h) have longer half-lives — prolonged toxicity.
Inline MCQ 2. Which β-blocker overdose is associated with QT prolongation and torsades de pointes due to Class III antiarrhythmic activity?
A. Atenolol
B. Metoprolol
C. Sotalol (also blocks K channels)
D. Esmolol
Answer: C. Sotalol = β-blocker + Class III antiarrhythmic (K-channel block) → QT prolongation, torsades. Reference: Tintinalli Table 194-2.

4. Clinical Features

Tintinalli Table 194-3 p.1272
📚 Table 194-3 — Common Findings With β-Blocker Toxicity (cardiovascular, CNS, pulmonary, electrolytes) (Tintinalli p.1272)

Cardiovascular (dominant)

  • Bradycardia + hypotension — most common.
  • AV blocks (1°, 2°, 3°) and conduction delays.
  • Asystole, ventricular dysrhythmias.
  • Wide QRS from Na-channel block (propranolol, acebutolol).
  • Decreased contractility → cardiogenic shock.
  • Sotalol: may also have hypoglycemia, prolonged QT, torsades.

CNS (lipophilic agents)

  • Depressed mental status, coma.
  • Seizures (especially propranolol).
  • Psychosis.
  • Respiratory depression / arrest.

Pulmonary

  • Bronchospasm (especially in asthmatics with non-selective agents).
  • Acute respiratory distress.

Metabolic

  • Hypoglycemia — especially in children, diabetics; β₂ block → ↓ glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis.
  • Hyperkalemia rare.
Onset of toxicity: usually within 1–2 hours of immediate-release ingestion; up to 6 hours with extended-release. Sotalol can have delayed peak (up to 12 h).

5. Diagnosis & Differential

Tintinalli Table 194-4 p.1272

Workup

  • ECG on arrival + continuous monitoring.
  • Glucose — fingerstick + serum (hypoglycemia common).
  • BMP, Mg²⁺ (especially for sotalol).
  • Serum lactate — high in cardiogenic shock.
  • APAP/salicylate level for co-ingestants.
  • β-blocker level NOT routinely available or useful.
  • Echocardiogram for severe cases (assess CO, EF).

Differential of toxic bradycardia + hypotension

📚 Table 194-4 — Toxicologic Causes of Bradycardia and Hypotension: differentiating features (Tintinalli p.1272)
CauseDistinguishing features
Calcium channel blockerHyperglycemia, lactate ↑↑, normal mentation early
β-blockerHypoglycemia (especially with propranolol/in children), CNS depression early (propranolol)
Cardiac glycosides (digoxin/oleander)Ventricular ectopy, bidirectional VT, hyperkalemia, may cross-react with digoxin assay
Class IC antiarrhythmics (propafenone)Wide-complex tachycardia, QRS widening
ClonidineOpioid-like: coma, miosis, decreased respirations
Cyanide (acute)Profound metabolic acidosis, ↑↑ lactate
Digoxin (acute)Hyperkalemia + dig assay positive
OrganophosphatesCholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE-M / DUMBBELS)
Pearl — CCB vs β-blocker: Both cause bradycardia + hypotension. Distinguishing labs: β-blocker → HYPOglycemia; CCB → HYPERglycemia (CCB inhibits insulin release from pancreatic β-cells via L-type Ca²⁺ channels).
Inline MCQ 3. Which laboratory finding helps distinguish β-blocker from calcium channel blocker overdose?
A. Hyperkalemia (β-blocker) vs Hypokalemia (CCB)
B. Wide QRS (β-blocker) vs Narrow QRS (CCB)
C. Hypocalcemia (β-blocker) vs Hypercalcemia (CCB)
D. Hypoglycemia (β-blocker, esp. children/propranolol) vs Hyperglycemia (CCB → impairs insulin release)
Answer: D. β-blocker → hypoglycemia (block β₂ glycogenolysis); CCB → hyperglycemia (block pancreatic L-type Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ insulin release). Reference: Tintinalli p.1272.

6. Treatment Algorithm

Tintinalli Fig 194-2 p.1273
📚 Fig 194-2 — Management strategies in β-blocker toxicity: by ECG/contractility/SVR/HR — directed therapy (Tintinalli p.1273)

General initial management

  1. ABCs — early intubation if obtunded; hemodynamic monitoring.
  2. IV access × 2; volume resuscitation 1–2 L NS bolus.
  3. Continuous cardiac monitoring.
  4. ECG — assess QRS width (Na block) and QT (sotalol).
  5. Pacing — transcutaneous if symptomatic bradycardia; transvenous if persistent.
  6. Atropine 0.5–1 mg IV — temporizing measure (often ineffective in significant β-blocker overdose).

Decontamination

  • Activated charcoal 1 g/kg within 1–2 h of ingestion (extended to 4 h for sustained-release).
  • Whole-bowel irrigation for sustained-release products.

Specific therapies

FindingTherapy
Bradycardia / hypotensionGlucagon (5 mg IV bolus → infusion); atropine (limited value)
Decreased contractilityHigh-dose insulin (HDI) + dextrose
Decreased SVR / hypotension despite contractilityVasopressors (NE, epi, vasopressin)
Wide QRS >120 ms (Na-channel block)Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg IV
Sotalol with QT prolongation/torsadesMagnesium sulfate; isoproterenol; overdrive pacing
Refractory shockIV lipid emulsion (if lipophilic agent); VA-ECMO
📚 Table 194-5 — Treatment Options for β-Blocker Toxicity (Tintinalli p.1273)
Sotalol-specific management:
• QT prolongation/torsades — magnesium sulfate 2 g IV
• Isoproterenol or overdrive pacing to shorten QT
• AVOID Class IA/III antiarrhythmics
• Hemodialysis CAN remove sotalol (small Vd, low protein binding) — consider in refractory cases

7. Glucagon — First-Line Antidote

Tintinalli p.1273

Mechanism

  • Bypasses β-receptor by directly activating cardiac glucagon receptors → ↑ adenylate cyclase → ↑ cAMP → ↑ contractility + ↑ heart rate.
  • Effective for both β-blocker and CCB overdose.
  • Onset 1–3 min; peak ~5 min; duration 10–15 min (short — needs infusion).

Dosing

  • Initial bolus: 3–10 mg IV over 1–2 min in adults (50–150 µg/kg).
  • Repeat: if no response in 5 min, can repeat × 2.
  • Maintenance infusion: rate equal to the effective bolus dose per hour (e.g., if 5 mg bolus worked → 5 mg/h infusion).
  • Pediatric: 50–150 µg/kg IV bolus.

Side effects

  • Nausea/vomiting very common (occurs in >50%) — pretreat with antiemetic; aspiration risk with airway compromise.
  • Hyperglycemia (mild).
  • Tachyphylaxis with prolonged use.
⚠️ Pearl — anticipated nausea/vomiting: nearly all patients given high-dose glucagon vomit. Pretreat with ondansetron 4–8 mg IV; intubate first if airway protection is uncertain.
Inline MCQ 4. Initial glucagon dose for severe β-blocker toxicity is:
A. 1 mg IV bolus once
B. 3–10 mg IV bolus, then infusion at the effective dose per hour
C. 50 mg IV bolus
D. Glucagon is contraindicated
Answer: B. Glucagon 3–10 mg IV bolus (50–150 µg/kg) → infusion. Pretreat with antiemetic. Reference: Tintinalli p.1273.

8. High-Dose Insulin (HDI) Therapy

Tintinalli p.1273

Indications

  • Significant β-blocker (or CCB) toxicity with reduced contractility.
  • Hemodynamic instability not responsive to glucagon and vasopressors alone.
  • Increasingly considered first-line ahead of glucagon in some institutions for severe cases.

Mechanism

  • Improves myocardial inotropy by altering myocyte energy substrate utilization (forces myocyte uptake of glucose for energy) — without raising heart rate or causing arrhythmia.
  • Dose-dependent improvement in cardiac output.

Dosing

  1. Bolus: regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV.
  2. Infusion: 1 unit/kg/h IV (titrate up to 10 units/kg/h based on response).
  3. Concurrent dextrose: D50 25 g IV bolus, then D10 or D20 infusion at 0.5 g/kg/h.
  4. Monitor glucose every 15–30 min; K⁺ every 1–2 h (will drop with insulin).
  5. Some institutions use continuous KCl infusion 20–40 mEq/h to maintain normokalemia.

Caveats

  • Onset of effect 15–60 min — slower than glucagon but more sustained.
  • Very high doses (10 units/kg/h) can be needed; some institutions go to 22 units/kg/h.
  • Watch for hypoglycemia (need continuous dextrose) and hypokalemia (continuous K⁺).
Pearl — HDI as preferred therapy: increasingly considered superior to glucagon in many severe β-blocker / CCB overdoses due to sustained cardiac output improvement. Many centers now skip glucagon and start HDI directly in severe cases. Both can be combined.

9. Refractory Cases — Beyond Standard Therapy

Tintinalli p.1273

Step-up therapy when standard fails

  1. IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid 20%):
    • Useful for lipid-soluble β-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol, carvedilol, nebivolol).
    • Mechanism: "lipid sink" sequesters lipophilic drug from cardiac tissue.
    • Dose: 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min × 30–60 min. Repeat bolus if needed.
  2. VA-ECMO:
    • For refractory cardiogenic shock unresponsive to medical therapy.
    • Bridge to drug clearance (especially for short half-life agents like esmolol or for HDI to take effect).
    • Increasingly used in toxicologic shock; consult cardiothoracic + poison control early.
  3. Pacing options:
    • Transcutaneous → transvenous → epicardial (if cardiac surgery).
    • May not capture in severe β-blocker overdose — consider ECMO first.
  4. Hemodialysis:
    • Effective for water-soluble β-blockers with low protein binding: atenolol, sotalol, nadolol, acebutolol.
    • NOT effective for lipophilic, highly protein-bound: propranolol, metoprolol, carvedilol.
  5. Sotalol-specific: torsades → magnesium 2 g IV + isoproterenol + overdrive pacing.
⚠️ Pearl — when to call ECMO: escalating vasopressors + glucagon + HDI + lipid emulsion failing → urgent VA-ECMO consult. Especially propranolol overdose (worst prognosis without ECMO bridge).
Inline MCQ 5. Which β-blocker is BEST removed by hemodialysis?
A. Propranolol (high lipophilicity, high protein binding)
B. Atenolol (low lipophilicity, low protein binding, water-soluble)
C. Carvedilol (large Vd)
D. Metoprolol (CYP-metabolized)
Answer: B. Atenolol (and sotalol, nadolol) are water-soluble + low Vd + low protein binding → dialyzable. Propranolol etc. are not. Reference: Tintinalli p.1273.

10. Disposition

Tintinalli p.1273
  • Discharge: very rare; only if asymptomatic + immediate-release agent + 6 hours of normal vitals + no symptoms + reliable disposition + psychiatric clearance for intentional ingestions.
  • Telemetry: any documented toxicity; mild bradycardia/hypotension that resolved.
  • ICU: active vasopressor/glucagon/HDI infusion, hemodynamic instability, severe dysrhythmias, sustained-release ingestion (12-h+ observation), sotalol toxicity.
  • Sustained-release: observe ≥12 h; sotalol ≥12 h.
  • Pediatric: "one pill can kill" applies; admit any toddler with confirmed/suspected ingestion of propranolol/sotalol.
  • Psychiatric consultation for intentional ingestions.

⚕️ ATLS 11th — β-Blocker Toxicity in Trauma

ATLS
  • β-blockers are among the most common cardiovascular medications — present in many elderly trauma patients.
  • Bradycardia + hypotension in trauma may not be entirely from hemorrhagic shock — consider β-blocker therapeutic effect.
  • Patients on chronic β-blocker may not mount typical compensatory tachycardia in hemorrhage — beware of underestimating shock severity.
  • Trauma + β-blocker overdose: severe bradycardia + hypotension + cardiogenic shock → escalate aggressively (HDI + glucagon + vasopressors + lipid emulsion + ECMO).
  • RSI considerations: ketamine acceptable; etomidate hemodynamically neutral; rocuronium for paralysis; avoid succinylcholine if hyperkalemia.
  • Glucagon + atropine as adjuncts in trauma + β-blocker.

📗 Rosen's EM 10th — β-Blocker Toxicity

Rosen's Ch.142
  • Same overall framework — glucagon as classical antidote; HDI increasingly first-line.
  • Rosen's emphasizes: propranolol is the most dangerous β-blocker overdose; aggressive multi-modal therapy + ECMO consultation early.
  • Sotalol toxicity: dialyzable; magnesium for torsades; isoproterenol; overdrive pacing.
  • HDI: may need very high doses (up to 10–22 units/kg/h); continuous dextrose + K⁺ replacement.
  • Lipid emulsion: recommended for lipophilic β-blocker overdose with hemodynamic compromise.
  • "One pill can kill" in toddlers: emphasized for sotalol, propranolol — admit + observe ≥24 h.
  • VA-ECMO: increasing role as bridge to drug clearance in severe cases.

A. Atenolol
B. Bisoprolol
C. Propranolol (lipid-soluble + Na-channel block + non-selective)

A. Atenolol
B. Metoprolol
C. Sotalol (also blocks K channels)
D. Bisoprolol
Answer: C. Sotalol = β-blocker + Class III. Torsades risk.
End MCQ 3. First-line antidote for severe β-blocker toxicity is:
A. Atropine
B. Glucagon (3–10 mg IV bolus → infusion)
C. Calcium chloride
D. Naloxone
Answer: B. Glucagon bypasses β-receptors via direct cAMP activation. Initial bolus 3–10 mg IV.
End MCQ 4. Which lab finding distinguishes β-blocker from CCB overdose?
A. Hyperkalemia
B. Wide QRS
C. β-blocker → hypoglycemia, CCB → hyperglycemia
D. Lactate
Answer: C. β-blocker → hypoglycemia (β₂ block ↓ glycogenolysis); CCB → hyperglycemia (block insulin release).
End MCQ 5. Which β-blockers are most amenable to hemodialysis?
A. Propranolol, metoprolol
B. Atenolol, sotalol, nadolol, acebutolol (water-soluble, low protein binding)
C. Carvedilol, labetalol
D. None
Answer: B. Water-soluble + low Vd + low protein binding = dialyzable.
End MCQ 6. Which β-blocker has Na-channel-blocking (membrane-stabilizing) effect causing wide QRS?
A. Atenolol
B. Propranolol (also acebutolol, betaxolol)
C. Esmolol
D. Bisoprolol
Answer: B. Propranolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, oxprenolol have Na-channel-blocking activity → wide QRS like TCA → NaHCO3 helpful.
End MCQ 7. Treatment for sotalol-induced torsades de pointes is:
A. Procainamide
B. Magnesium 2 g IV + isoproterenol or overdrive pacing
C. β-agonist alone
D. CCB
Answer: B. Mg²⁺ stabilizes; isoproterenol (β-agonism shortens QT); overdrive pacing prevents pause-induced TdP.
End MCQ 8. Initial high-dose insulin (HDI) loading dose is:
A. 0.1 unit/kg IV
B. 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then 1 unit/kg/h infusion (titrate up to 10)
C. 100 units IV bolus
D. Insulin contraindicated
Answer: B. Insulin 1 unit/kg bolus, then 1 unit/kg/h infusion + concurrent dextrose. Titrate up to 10 unit/kg/h.
End MCQ 9. Why must dextrose be given concurrently with HDI?
A. Dextrose treats β-blocker toxicity
B. To prevent hypoglycemia from high-dose insulin
C. To reduce K⁺
D. Required for diagnosis
Answer: B. HDI delivers high insulin doses → hypoglycemia must be prevented with continuous dextrose infusion.
End MCQ 10. Onset of glucagon's hemodynamic effect after IV bolus is:
A. <30 seconds
B. 1–3 minutes
C. 30 minutes
D. 2 hours
Answer: B. Glucagon onset 1–3 min, peak ~5 min, duration 10–15 min — needs maintenance infusion.
End MCQ 11. Why is ondansetron given BEFORE glucagon?
A. Prevents allergic reaction
B. Prevents nausea/vomiting in >50% of glucagon doses (aspiration risk)
C. Synergistic effect
D. Routine for any IV med
Answer: B. Glucagon causes severe nausea/vomiting → aspiration risk; pretreat with antiemetic.
End MCQ 12. Which β-blocker class causes hypoglycemia most prominently in pediatrics?
A. β₁-selective (atenolol)
B. Non-selective (propranolol — blocks β₂ → ↓ glycogenolysis)
C. Combined α/β (labetalol)
D. None
Answer: B. β₂-block → ↓ glycogenolysis + ↓ gluconeogenesis. Children + diabetics most affected.
End MCQ 13. Sustained-release β-blocker observation period in ED:
A. 1 hour
B. 4 hours
C. ≥12 hours
D. 1 week
Answer: C. Sustained-release products may have delayed peak — observe ≥12 h. Sotalol also ≥12 h.
End MCQ 14. Which β-blocker has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA) that can mitigate bradycardia in overdose?
A. Propranolol
B. Pindolol, acebutolol, oxprenolol (partial agonists)
C. Sotalol
D. Esmolol
Answer: B. Pindolol/acebutolol/oxprenolol partial agonism may produce tachycardia/HTN (rather than bradycardia) in overdose.
End MCQ 15. Lipid emulsion 20% is most useful for which β-blocker overdose?
A. Atenolol (water-soluble)
B. Propranolol or carvedilol (lipid-soluble)
C. Sotalol
D. None
Answer: B. Lipid emulsion sequesters lipid-soluble drugs (propranolol, carvedilol, metoprolol).
End MCQ 16. Sotalol toxicity unique features include:
A. Hypoglycemia only
B. QT prolongation, torsades, dialyzable
C. Hyperthermia
D. Hyperkalemia
Answer: B. Sotalol causes both β-block and Class III antiarrhythmic effects. Dialyzable.
End MCQ 17. In refractory β-blocker shock failing all medical therapy, the next escalation is:
A. Rest and observe
B. VA-ECMO + continued aggressive medical therapy
C. Stop all drugs
D. Add another β-blocker
Answer: B. VA-ECMO bridge to drug clearance. Continued vasopressors + HDI + lipid emulsion.
End MCQ 18. Atropine in significant β-blocker overdose:
A. Always effective
B. Often INeffective (β-blockade overrides vagal effect); temporizing only
C. Indicated only in mild cases
D. Contraindicated
Answer: B. Atropine often fails in significant β-blocker overdose; temporizing while glucagon/HDI take effect.
End MCQ 19. A patient with severe propranolol overdose has wide QRS 140 ms + bradycardia. Best initial therapy:
A. Procainamide
B. NaHCO3 1–2 mEq/kg + glucagon + HDI + lipid emulsion
C. Adenosine
D. β-agonist nebulizer
Answer: B. Wide QRS = Na-channel block → NaHCO3. Combined with glucagon + HDI + lipid emulsion (lipophilic).
End MCQ 20. 'One pill can kill' β-blockers in toddlers include:
A. Atenolol only
B. Propranolol and sotalol especially
C. Acebutolol
D. None — pediatric β-blocker overdose is benign
Answer: B. Single tablets of propranolol/sotalol can be lethal in toddlers due to size + potency. Admit any pediatric ingestion.

🔑 Key Points (High-Yield)

  1. Cardiovascular dominant: bradycardia + hypotension + AV blocks.
  2. Propranolol = worst overdose: lipid-soluble (CNS toxicity, seizures) + Na-channel block (wide QRS) + non-selective.
  3. Sotalol = β-block + Class III antiarrhythmic → QT prolongation + torsades.
  4. β-blocker → HYPOglycemia (β₂ block ↓ glycogenolysis); CCB → HYPERglycemia (impairs insulin release). Distinguishing feature.
  5. Glucagon 3–10 mg IV bolus → infusion. First-line antidote. Pretreat with ondansetron (severe N/V).
  6. HDI 1 unit/kg bolus → 1 unit/kg/h + continuous dextrose + K⁺ replacement. Titrate up to 10 unit/kg/h. Increasingly first-line in severe cases.
  7. NaHCO3 1–2 mEq/kg for wide QRS (Na-channel-blocking β-blockers: propranolol, acebutolol, betaxolol).
  8. Sotalol torsades: Mg 2 g IV + isoproterenol + overdrive pacing.
  9. Lipid emulsion for refractory lipid-soluble β-blocker overdose (propranolol, carvedilol, metoprolol).
  10. VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock — bridge to drug clearance.
  11. Hemodialysis effective for atenolol, sotalol, nadolol, acebutolol (water-soluble); NOT for propranolol, metoprolol, carvedilol.
  12. Atropine often INeffective in significant β-blocker overdose — temporizing only.
  13. "One pill can kill" — pediatric ingestion of propranolol/sotalol; admit any toddler.
  14. Sustained-release ingestion → observe ≥12 h; sotalol ≥12 h.
  15. ISA agents (pindolol, acebutolol, oxprenolol) may produce tachycardia/HTN rather than bradycardia in overdose.
